# Game Design Seven composable agent skills for creating and revising playable games. [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.1.1-informational?style=flat-square)](VERSION)
Use Game Design with an AI agent to work on the rules, encounters, clues, worlds and systems of your game. Start with a current artifact and a specific change, or develop a new concept into something a participant can play or express. The result can be a revised rule, scene, map, resource model, paper episode, game data or prototype; a large design document is optional. To work on your game, [choose a skill](#what-you-can-do) and follow the [quick start](#quick-start). To explore the methods first, open a [playable example](#demonstration). ## What you can do | Work on | Start with | | --- | --- | | A new concept, a change spanning several systems, or adaptation to another language or device | [game-design](skills/game-design/SKILL.md) | | Actions, timing, actor knowledge, spaces, encounters or free audiovisual play | [gameplay-design](skills/gameplay-design/SKILL.md) | | Clues and inference, learning, or assistance that helps someone act | [game-information-design](skills/game-information-design/SKILL.md) | | World relationships, characters, conditional scenes and expressive consequences | [game-world-narrative-design](skills/game-world-narrative-design/SKILL.md) | | Resources, access, progression, loss and recovery, or game state transfer | [game-systems-design](skills/game-systems-design/SKILL.md) | | Joint decisions, matching, accessibility, stopping and returning, or paid rights | [game-participation-design](skills/game-participation-design/SKILL.md) | | Authored content, generation, selection and the variety players encounter | [game-content-design](skills/game-content-design/SKILL.md) | Use any entry directly when it fits the task. Use `game-design` when the overall direction or the interaction between decisions needs work. Scores, victory conditions and simulation are optional. Permanent assistance, purposeful repetition and an accepted ending can be legitimate design choices. ## Demonstration [East Gate](examples/adaptation/README.md) is a small CLI game showing how to adapt an existing puzzle across language and layout. The English four-line verse spells EAST; the Russian six-line version spells ВОСТОК. The target shows one line at a time and lets players pin whole lines for comparison. Players still find and choose the direction. A correct choice opens the gate and awards a token needed by a later ferry scene. A wrong direction returns to the verse without loss. A broken acrostic or mismatched later sign is rejected before play. These different outcomes make the example useful for inspecting whether an adaptation preserves the connection between information, action and consequence. [Run it below](#run-east-gate). For other kinds of work, explore: - [Playable design studies](docs/examples.md): paper examples of encounters, expressive play, worlds, learning, resources and cooperative campaigns. - [Godot episode](examples/godot-episode/README.md): native input, timing and physics in a small game. - [Analysis lab](examples/analysis-lab/README.md): resource access, save migration, actor-specific views, content selection and telemetry. ## Access Clone or download the [source repository](https://github.com/Muratovnik/gamedesign-skills), or use a versioned source archive as described in the [installation guide](docs/installation.md#prepare-a-versioned-source). Keep the **complete seven-skill bundle** together: entries use sibling references and runtime resources, so installing one skill directory on its own is not supported. For direct use, put the source in a location your agent is authorized to read. An explicit source read needs no client registration. Reading methods and paper examples needs only a text reader; reading a skill does not download or install runtime dependencies. General research and engineering methods come from the separately maintained [Assay](https://github.com/Muratovnik/assay) collection. Game Design does not install or embed it. When an operation requires an Assay method, supply the complete authorized source for **Assay 0.17.2**, commit `94c517b0aac9ba2575086bf9aead1cc828aadb0d`, and read that method under the [consumer and Assay contract](skills/game-design/references/consumer-and-assay-contract.md). Do not substitute another revision or bypass a disabled provider. If a required source is unavailable or incompatible, the dependent operation cannot proceed; independent game-design work may continue within that limit. The source also includes Codex and Claude Code plugin packaging under `game-design@game-design-source`. The [native installation guide](docs/installation.md) covers scope, conflicts, updates, disabling, removal and rollback. Native installation, discovery and lifecycle remain [unverified for the documented client builds](docs/compatibility.md#native-client-qualification). Client settings and publication require separate owner authorization. ## Quick start ### Apply a skill to your game Give your agent the absolute Game Design root, the game root, the current artifact and revision, the intended change, and the permitted work. Ask it to read the chosen `SKILL.md` and the references needed for that task. For example, replace the paths and encounter brief below with your own: ```text Game Design root: /absolute/game-design Game root: /absolute/my-game Current artifact: /absolute/my-game/design/bridge-encounter.md Revision: use the current contents of that file Allowed work: read the supplied sources and draft a revised encounter Read skills/gameplay-design/SKILL.md under the Game Design root and its relevant references. Revise the encounter so the warning leaves the player time to take an available response before the hazard arrives. Preserve the encounter's purpose and follow the timing change through its consequences. Return the revised encounter, the reason for the change, and what still needs to be checked in the running game or with players. ``` ### Run East Gate With a local source copy and **Python 3.11 or newer**, run this Bash example from the repository root. It uses Python's standard library. Choose a fresh output filename before each run. ```bash python3 examples/adaptation/consumer.py \ --artifact examples/adaptation/fixtures/east-gate-ru.json \ --expect-revision east-gate-ru-2 \ --pin 1 --pin 2 --pin 3 --pin 4 --pin 5 --pin 6 \ --choose east \ --output /tmp/east-gate-result.json ``` The command replays pinning all six Russian lines and choosing east. Inspect the JSON result's notebook, open gate and token. The [East Gate guide](examples/adaptation/README.md) shows how to request individual line views, try a wrong direction, and pass the saved result to the ferry scene, which consumes the token. These are serialized text views and game actions; the example does not provide a rendered mobile interface. For package checks or release preparation, use the [development setup](#development-setup). ## Documentation - [Example guide](docs/examples.md): choose a study and follow its game relations. - [Capability map](docs/traceability.md): methods, examples and implementation boundaries. - [Consumer and Assay contract](skills/game-design/references/consumer-and-assay-contract.md): source binding, required methods and current game context. - [Environment contract](skills/game-design/references/environment-contracts.md): inputs, actions, outputs, consumers and precision limits. - [Compatibility](docs/compatibility.md): dependencies and the scope of client and runtime support. - [Design decisions](docs/decisions.md) and [research and evidence limits](docs/late-comparison.md). - [Russian quick start](docs/quickstart.ru.md). ## Limits The examples are authored development material. Their calculations and deterministic checks establish specific content, input, timing, geometry and state properties. They do not establish enjoyment, perception, learning, cultural interpretation or voluntary social consent. No model-quality improvement, user playtest or support for arbitrary engines is claimed. Use evidence from the relevant game, runtime or participants when those questions matter to your design. ## Contributing See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for method ownership, source-based changes and scoped checks. [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) records release changes; [release preparation](docs/releases.md) covers source archives and publication. ### Development setup From the repository root, create an isolated environment with Python 3.11 or newer and install the development dependencies. On Unix: ```bash python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt ``` On Windows, use `.venv/Scripts/python.exe` as the environment's interpreter. Run the relevant checks from the contribution guide and example READMEs with that interpreter. The Godot episode requires a separately obtained engine; see its README for the runtime and command. ## License The original methods, code and examples are licensed under [MIT](LICENSE). The redistributed technical plugin schema uses Apache-2.0; see [NOTICE.md](NOTICE.md) for its attribution and license. The package license does not cover linked research text, games or artwork.

# Foldnote

Foldnote turns a folder of workshop notes into one Markdown handout that you can share or print from your Markdown editor.

## Quick start

You need Python 3.11 or later. Foldnote uses only the Python standard library and runs directly from the release folder.

Open a terminal in the release folder containing `foldnote.py`, then run:

```sh
python foldnote.py build examples/notes handout.md
```

This creates `handout.md` in the current folder from the supplied example notes. Open it in your Markdown editor to review, share or print the handout.

## Use your own notes

Replace `examples/notes` in the command with your notes folder and `handout.md` with your chosen output path. Keep the output outside the input folder.

Foldnote reads Markdown files from the input folder and its subfolders, assembles them in relative-path order, and adds a heading showing each input path. Numbered filenames such as `01-welcome.md` and `02-tools.md` can order notes within a folder. The input notes stay unchanged.

If your output file already exists, choose a new filename or add `--replace` when you mean to overwrite it.

## Output format

The handout is a Markdown file; Foldnote has no PDF output. Image references remain as written in the notes, and image files are not copied.

## Documentation

- [Using Foldnote](docs/using-foldnote.md) describes the command and output behavior.
- [Contributing](docs/contributing.md) explains how to work on the tool itself.

# Foldnote

Foldnote turns a folder of Markdown workshop notes into one handout you can share
or print from your Markdown editor.

## Quick start

You need Python 3.11 or later. Foldnote uses only Python's standard library and
runs directly from the release folder.

1. Open a terminal in the release folder containing `foldnote.py`.
2. Build a handout from the included example notes:

   ```sh
   python foldnote.py build examples/notes handout.md
   ```

3. Open the new `handout.md` file in that same folder in your Markdown editor to
   review, share or print it.

Foldnote reads `.md` files in the notes folder and its subfolders, orders them by
relative path, and adds a heading showing each input file's path. It leaves the
input notes unchanged.

## Use your own notes

Replace `examples/notes` in the command with the path to your notes folder, and
choose an output path outside that folder. For example, if your notes are in a
folder named `my-notes` inside the release folder, run:

```sh
python foldnote.py build my-notes workshop-handout.md
```

For notes in the same folder, filename prefixes such as `01-welcome.md` and
`02-tools.md` let you set their order in the handout.

Existing output files are protected by default. Choose a new output filename, or
add `--replace` to the command when you intend to overwrite an existing handout.

The output is Markdown, not a PDF. Image references remain as written in the
notes, and Foldnote does not copy image files. If your notes include images, check
that the references work from the handout's location before sharing it.

## Documentation

- [Using Foldnote](docs/using-foldnote.md) covers the command and output behavior.
- [Contributing](docs/contributing.md) explains how to run the tests when changing
  the tool.

# Restart-safe synchronization

Resume a Kite Ledger consumer from its last durably saved cursor. To make that
cursor safe to reuse, commit the corresponding local work before or together with
the checkpoint. Record each processed event's identity in the same transaction as
its local change, so that a delivery seen again after a restart can be skipped
without losing a distinct event.

## What a cursor tells you

The [feed contract](feed-contract.md) defines an ordered sequence of accepted
events. Each event has a monotonically increasing cursor. Requesting events
after cursor `C` returns events whose cursors are greater than `C`, in order,
up to the requested page limit. The response's `next_cursor` is the cursor of
its last event. An empty response returns `C` as `next_cursor`.

Receiving `next_cursor` does not mean those events have been written to your
database. It is a position for a later request; your consumer decides when to
save it as a checkpoint. The checkpoint must become durable together with or
after the local work it covers. Every event in the page must be applied in
that commit or already have been processed. Otherwise, a restart could resume
beyond work that never reached the local copy.

Cursors are opaque tokens. Store and resend the token you receive; do not
increment it or calculate a position from it. Names such as `c40` below are
illustrative.

## Recognize an event by its identity

Every accepted event has an immutable `event_id`, unique within its feed. A
repeated delivery retains that ID. Use `(feed_id, event_id)` as the key in your
processed-event records when consuming several feeds, because different feeds
can reuse an `event_id`. For a single feed, `event_id` is sufficient within
that feed's records.

Payload equality does not identify a repeated delivery. Two accepted events
can have the same item, value and timestamp while having different event IDs.
Process both. For example, setting an item to the same value twice may leave
the same final item state, but a count of accepted events must increase twice.
Deduplicating by payload or timestamp would incorrectly discard one event.

## Commit local work and progress safely

The contract supports two local storage arrangements:

| Arrangement | Commit boundary | Behavior after a crash |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One transaction for a page | Commit the page's local changes, processed IDs and `next_cursor` together. | A committed page has a matching checkpoint. An uncommitted page can be fetched and processed again. |
| Separate checkpoint write | Commit each local change with its processed ID, then save `next_cursor` after the whole page is accounted for. | Some changes may be committed while the checkpoint still points to an earlier position. Replayed IDs let the consumer recognize that work. |

In either arrangement, the deduplication check belongs inside the transaction
that applies a previously unseen event and records its ID. The change and the
processed-ID record must commit together. Saving an ID first could cause a
restart to skip a change that never committed; saving the change without its
ID could cause that change to be applied again.

For the separate-checkpoint arrangement, use this loop:

1. Load the saved cursor for the feed and fetch a page after it.
2. Visit the returned events in order. For each event, begin a local transaction
   and check its identity in the processed-event records. If it is already
   recorded, skip its local change. Otherwise, apply the change and record its
   identity in that transaction. Commit the transaction before moving to the
   next event.
3. After every event in the page is durably applied or already recorded, save
   the returned `next_cursor`. If an event cannot be processed, stop processing
   the page and leave the checkpoint unchanged.
4. Fetch the next page after the saved cursor. On an empty response, the cursor
   stays the same.

On restart, run the same loop from the saved cursor. A crash between committing
local work and saving the checkpoint leaves the checkpoint behind that work.
The next request therefore asks for some of the same events again. This follows
from the saved position and the feed's request rules; it does not mean new
events were accepted. The processed-ID records make that replay safe for the
local changes. There is no transaction spanning the feed service and your local
database.

## Worked example: two matching payloads and one restart

In this single-feed example from the [consumer notes](../notes/consumer-design.md),
the saved cursor is `c40` and neither event below is recorded as processed.
A request after `c40` returns this page with `next_cursor` equal to `c42`:

| Event ID | Cursor | Item | Value | Timestamp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e41` | `c41` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |
| `e42` | `c42` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |

The consumer uses separate checkpoint writes:

1. It applies `e41` and records `e41` in one local transaction. That transaction
   commits. If the local work includes an event count, the count increases by one.
2. The process exits before applying `e42` and before saving `c42`. The durable
   checkpoint is still `c40`, and only `e41` has a processed-ID record.
3. After restart, the consumer requests events after `c40`. It receives `e41`
   and `e42` again.
4. It checks `e41` inside a local transaction, finds its processed-ID record and
   skips its change. The event count does not increase.
5. It checks `e42`, finds no record, and commits `e42`'s local change and ID
   together. The event count increases by one, even though `e42`'s payload
   matches `e41`'s payload.
6. Both events are now accounted for, so it saves `c42`. The next request uses
   that token and returns events after `c42`.

The two deliveries of `e41` represent one accepted event. The different IDs
`e41` and `e42` represent two accepted events. The final local item value is `6`,
and the example contributes two events to a local event count. If the process
exits again after committing `e42` but before saving `c42`, another replay
finds both IDs already recorded and applies neither change again.

## Recover when the saved cursor has expired

Events remain available for 72 hours after server acceptance. If the saved
cursor is before the available history, the server returns `history_expired`.
Resume by obtaining a [fresh snapshot](snapshot.md) with its matching feed
cursor, replacing the local copy with the snapshot state, and installing that
state and cursor together as one local checkpoint. Then request events after
the snapshot's cursor.

A snapshot rebuilds the current materialized state. It cannot reconstruct
expired event history, so it cannot recover a count or other historical result
that requires those missing events.

# Restart-safe synchronization

To maintain a local copy from the Kite Ledger event feed, resume from a durable
checkpoint and record each processed event's identity with its local change. A
restart can deliver an event again when its change committed before the checkpoint
moved. The recorded identity lets you recognize that delivery and skip work you
have already committed.

## Keep feed position and event identity separate

The [feed contract](feed-contract.md) gives each accepted event two identifiers
with different jobs:

| Field | Purpose in the consumer |
| --- | --- |
| Cursor | Identifies a position in the ordered feed. Save it as a checkpoint to choose where the next request starts. |
| `event_id` | Identifies one accepted event. Record it to recognize repeated deliveries. |

A request after cursor `C` returns events with cursors greater than `C`, in order,
up to the requested page limit. The response's `next_cursor` is the cursor of its
last event; an empty response returns `C` as `next_cursor`. This is a position for
the next request, not an acknowledgement that your local writes have committed.

Cursors increase monotonically, but clients treat them as opaque tokens. Store
and resend the tokens returned by the service without arithmetic. The short
cursor names in the example below are illustrative.

An `event_id` is immutable and unique within its feed. Repeated delivery of an
event keeps that ID. If you consume several feeds, use `(feed_id, event_id)` as the
deduplication key because different feeds can reuse an `event_id`.

Payload fields cannot identify a delivery: two distinct accepted events can have
the same item, value and timestamp. Comparing those fields, or hashing the payload,
would incorrectly collapse such events. Use the event identity to decide whether
to apply an event; use its payload to determine the local change.

## Resume from committed local work

Keep three things in durable storage for each feed: the local copy, the processed
event identities and the saved cursor. If you are starting without a checkpoint,
install a [fresh snapshot](snapshot.md) and its matching feed cursor together as
one local checkpoint. On a restart, load your saved cursor and request events
after it.

The following loop uses the arrangement in the
[consumer notes](../notes/consumer-design.md), where each event commits before the
page checkpoint:

1. Fetch a page after the saved cursor.
2. Handle the returned events in order. For each event, use one local transaction
   to check its deduplication key. If the key is already recorded, skip the local
   change. Otherwise, apply the change and record the key in that same transaction.
3. After every event in the page has either committed or been recognized as
   already processed, durably save the response's `next_cursor` as the checkpoint.
4. Fetch the next page after that saved cursor. An empty page leaves the checkpoint
   unchanged.

If an event fails to commit, stop processing that page and leave the page
checkpoint unchanged. Resume from the saved cursor; any earlier events whose
transactions committed will be recognized when they return.

The transaction boundary is essential. Saving the checkpoint before the
corresponding changes commit can make a restart skip unapplied events. Recording
an event as processed before its local change commits creates the same problem:
the next delivery would be skipped even though the change was lost. The identity
check, local change and processed-ID record must succeed or roll back together.

The [contract](feed-contract.md) also supports committing a whole page's local
changes, processed IDs and checkpoint in one local transaction. Keep the same
identity checks inside that transaction. A restart then sees either the old
checkpoint and local state or the committed page and its new checkpoint. Choose
the transaction arrangement your local store supports; there is no transaction
spanning the feed service and your database.

## Worked example: a crash partway through a page

This example follows the supplied [consumer trace](../notes/consumer-design.md)
for a single feed. The saved checkpoint is `c40`. A request after `c40` returns:

| Event ID | Cursor | Item | Value | Timestamp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e41` | `c41` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |
| `e42` | `c42` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |

The response has `next_cursor = c42`. Both payloads match, but the different IDs
identify two separate accepted events. To make their effects visible, suppose
your local transaction also increments a counter for each newly processed event.
The count below covers only these two events.

| Step | Durable local result | Saved checkpoint | Count |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Receive the page | Neither event has been applied or recorded yet. | `c40` | 0 |
| Commit `e41` | Apply its change, increment the counter and record `e41` together. | `c40` | 1 |
| Process exits | `e42` has not been applied; the checkpoint has not moved. | `c40` | 1 |
| Restart and fetch after `c40` | The service returns `e41` and `e42` again. | `c40` | 1 |
| Handle returned `e41` | Its ID is recorded, so skip its change and counter increment. | `c40` | 1 |
| Commit returned `e42` | Its ID is new, so apply its change, increment the counter and record `e42` together. | `c40` | 2 |
| Save `next_cursor` | Both events have been handled; save `c42`. | `c42` | 2 |

The next request starts after `c42`. Each event has contributed once to the local
counter despite appearing in two responses. Looking only at `shelf-A = 6` would
hide this distinction: identical final item state does not mean there was only
one event.

If another crash happens after `e42` commits but before `c42` is saved, the next
restart requests after `c40` again. Both IDs are now recorded, so both local
changes are skipped before the checkpoint advances. Repeated delivery is safe
because the effects and the evidence that they happened are durable together.
This protects the changes included in the local transaction while allowing the
feed to deliver events repeatedly.

## Recover when history has expired

Events remain available for **72 hours after server acceptance**. If your saved
cursor is before the available history, the service returns `history_expired`.
Recover using the [snapshot procedure](snapshot.md):

1. Obtain a fresh snapshot with its matching feed cursor.
2. Replace the local copy with the snapshot and install that cursor together as
   one local checkpoint.
3. Continue fetching events after the snapshot's cursor.

The snapshot rebuilds the current materialized state. It cannot reconstruct
expired event history or let you replay those individual events. A successful
state rebuild therefore does not prove that every expired event was processed.

# Foldnote first-use review

The release-folder onboarding and project descriptions need revision for a workshop organizer using Foldnote for the first time. The existing plain Markdown presentation fits the adopted style.

## Findings and proposed corrections

### 1. Medium: the README starts with contributor setup

[README.md](README.md), under “Get started,” tells readers to clone the repository, read the contributing guide and run tests before an unspecified build command. An organizer already receiving the release folder has no direct route from this page to a handout. The existing [usage guide](docs/using-foldnote.md) documents direct script execution, and [the contributing guide](docs/contributing.md) distinguishes that route from development in a source checkout.

Replace this paragraph with the release-folder path: require Python 3.11 or later, tell readers to open a terminal in the folder containing `foldnote.py`, then show:

    python foldnote.py build examples/notes handout.md

Explain that this creates `handout.md` in the current folder. Link to [Using Foldnote](docs/using-foldnote.md) for using their own notes, ordering and image limitations. Keep the output-path and replacement guidance visible: choose an output outside the input folder; an existing output is protected unless `--replace` is deliberately supplied. State that Foldnote produces Markdown and does not create PDFs; readers can print the handout from their Markdown editor. Put the contributor link after the first-use instructions and label its development purpose.

### 2. Medium: the opening and listing descriptions omit the useful outcome

The README’s opening leads with six sample notes and three unit tests. The `description` in [repository.json](repository.json) and `[project].description` in [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml) both describe “a Markdown tool with six bundled example notes.” Those counts match the supplied examples and test source, but they do not explain what an organizer can accomplish and will need maintenance if the inventory changes.

The [release handoff](notes/handoff.md) identifies the main use as turning workshop notes into one handout; [the implementation](foldnote.py) supports that behavior. Replace the README opening with:

> Foldnote combines a folder of workshop notes into one Markdown handout you can share or print from your Markdown editor.

Use this shorter description in both metadata fields:

> Combine a folder of workshop notes into one Markdown handout.

The examples remain useful in the first-use command; their exact count and the test count do not need to define the product.

### 3. Low: the final README paragraph does not help first use

The training-afternoon origin and May folder reorganization in the final paragraph are supported by [the handoff](notes/handoff.md), but neither changes the organizer’s current setup, command or result. Omit that paragraph from the README. The background already exists in the handoff; no new history document is needed.

## Verification and scope

Reviewed the three requested files against the supplied usage, contributing and handoff documents, implementation, examples and test source. The Python requirement agrees across the usage guide and `pyproject.toml`. The sample build command above exited successfully in the copied folder and produced a handout with all six sample headings in relative-path order. Its temporary output was removed. Tests were read, not run; package installation and publication were outside this review. Only this review was added; product files were not edited.

# Game Design Agent skills for turning game ideas and revisions into playable rules, scenes and systems. [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-0.1.1-informational?style=flat-square)](VERSION)
Use Game Design with an agent to develop a new game or work on an existing one. Each skill provides a procedure for reading the current material, making a concrete change and following its consequences into related parts of the game. The result can be a rule, map, encounter, scene, resource model, playable paper episode or running prototype. A full game design document is optional. You can also browse the examples to see how the methods apply to actual rules, content and game state, from paper studies to Python consumers and a Godot episode. ## What you can do | Skill | Use it to | | --- | --- | | [game-design](skills/game-design/SKILL.md) | Develop a concept, connect changes across systems, or adapt a game to another language or device. | | [gameplay-design](skills/gameplay-design/SKILL.md) | Shape actions, timing, spatial opportunities, encounters and expressive audiovisual play. | | [game-information-design](skills/game-information-design/SKILL.md) | Build inference paths, learning sequences and assistance that supports the intended task. | | [game-world-narrative-design](skills/game-world-narrative-design/SKILL.md) | Develop world relationships, character knowledge, conditional scenes and dramatic consequences. | | [game-systems-design](skills/game-systems-design/SKILL.md) | Design resource access, development, loss, recovery and transfers of game state. | | [game-participation-design](skills/game-participation-design/SKILL.md) | Work on joint decisions, matching, accessible action, stopping and returning, and paid rights. | | [game-content-design](skills/game-content-design/SKILL.md) | Build a repertoire and preserve meaningful relationships through generation, selection and presentation. | Choose an entry directly for a focused task, or combine entries when a change crosses their boundaries. The methods allow expressive play without victory conditions, permanent assistance, purposeful repetition and an accepted ending. ## Demonstration Start with [East Gate](examples/adaptation/README.md), a small puzzle adapted from English into Russian and from a complete verse into a one-line display. Players can permanently pin whole lines for comparison, infer the answer and choose one of four directions. The saved direction and token also matter to a later ferry scene. With a complete local checkout and **Python 3.11 or newer**, run this from the repository root. Replace `/tmp/east-gate-result.json` with a new, writable output path on your machine: ```bash python3 examples/adaptation/consumer.py --artifact examples/adaptation/fixtures/east-gate-ru.json --expect-revision east-gate-ru-2 --pin 1 --pin 2 --pin 3 --pin 4 --pin 5 --pin 6 --choose east --output /tmp/east-gate-result.json ``` This command supplies the pin and direction actions. Inspect the result's notebook, open gate and token. A wrong direction is a valid retry; a broken acrostic or later sign is rejected as invalid content. The [example README](examples/adaptation/README.md) shows how to view individual lines and use the saved result in the ferry consumer. For other kinds of work, explore the [Godot input and physics episode](examples/godot-episode/README.md), the [analysis lab](examples/analysis-lab/README.md) for resources, saves, actor views and content selection, or the [example guide](docs/examples.md) for playable paper studies. ## Access Use a complete local checkout or extracted source archive. **All seven skill directories form the supported bundle**: keep their sibling references and runtime resources together, even when using only one entry. The [installation guide](docs/installation.md) covers source identity and archive verification. For direct use, give your agent the authorized absolute paths to Game Design and your game, and have it read the applicable `SKILL.md` and references. This route needs a text reader and does not require client registration. Reading a skill does not install dependencies or authorize commands, edits or changes to client settings. General research and engineering procedures come from the separately maintained [Assay](https://github.com/Muratovnik/assay) collection. When the task requires one of those methods, supply a separately obtained, authorized Assay source. The shipped binding requires **Assay 0.17.2**, commit `94c517b0aac9ba2575086bf9aead1cc828aadb0d`. Game Design does not bundle or install Assay. Read the applicable method and references through the [consumer and Assay contract](skills/game-design/references/consumer-and-assay-contract.md), which includes the source verifier. Do not bypass a disabled provider. If a required resource is unavailable or incompatible, the dependent operation must stop; independent design work can continue with that limit stated. Generated Codex and Claude Code marketplaces identify the bundle as `game-design@game-design-source`. Their native installation and lifecycle remain **unverified**. Before choosing that route, read the [client qualification limits](docs/compatibility.md#native-client-qualification) and follow the [installation and lifecycle procedures](docs/installation.md) for the client's identity, scope, conflicts, updates and rollback. Installation and settings changes require the installation owner's authorization. ## Quick start To apply a skill to your own game: 1. Choose a current artifact, such as a puzzle, encounter, map, scene or resource table, and describe the change you want. 2. Give the agent the Game Design root, game root and relevant artifact paths. State the game's constraints and which reads, edits or commands are allowed. 3. Ask it to read the matching skill and relevant references, then return a usable revised artifact, the reason for the change and any observations still needed to assess it. For example, adapt this request to a puzzle in your game. Replace the paths, goal and permissions with your actual ones: ```text Game Design source: /absolute/game-design Game source: /absolute/my-game Current artifact: /absolute/my-game/design/gate-puzzle.md Read skills/game-information-design/SKILL.md in Game Design and the references needed for this task. # Foldnote

Foldnote turns a folder of workshop notes into one Markdown handout that you can share or print from your Markdown editor.

## Quick start

You need Python 3.11 or later. Foldnote uses only Python's standard library and runs directly from the release folder.

Open a terminal in the release folder, where `foldnote.py` is located, and run:

```sh
python foldnote.py build examples/notes handout.md
```

This creates `handout.md` in the release folder from the bundled example notes. Open it in your Markdown editor to review, share or print it.

Foldnote reads `.md` files from the input folder and its subfolders. It combines them in relative-path order, with a heading showing each input path. The input notes stay unchanged.

## Use your own notes

Replace `my-notes` below with the path to your notes folder. Choose an output path outside that folder so a later build does not include an earlier handout:

```sh
python foldnote.py build my-notes workshop-handout.md
```

Here, `workshop-handout.md` is created in the current folder. If the output already exists, Foldnote stops without overwriting it. Choose a new filename, or add `--replace` when you intend to replace that output:

```sh
python foldnote.py build my-notes workshop-handout.md --replace
```

## Output limits

Foldnote produces Markdown; it does not generate PDFs. Image references remain as written in the notes, and Foldnote does not copy image files.

## Documentation

- [Using Foldnote](docs/using-foldnote.md)
- [Contributing](docs/contributing.md) — instructions for changing the tool.

# Restart-safe synchronization

To build a local copy from the Kite Ledger event feed, keep a durable feed checkpoint and a record of the events whose local changes have committed. After a restart, request events after that checkpoint and use the processed event IDs to recognize work already committed. The checkpoint can lag behind local work, so the consumer must be able to receive an event again without applying it twice.

## Feed position and event identity

The [feed contract](feed-contract.md) gives each accepted event a cursor and an immutable `event_id`. These serve different purposes:

| Field | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Cursor | A position in one ordered feed, used to resume requests. |
| `event_id` | The identity of one accepted event, used to recognize repeated delivery. It is unique within its feed. |
| Payload | The event's data. Matching item, value and timestamp do not establish that two deliveries are the same event. |

For a consumer of several feeds, use `(feed_id, event_id)` as the delivery deduplication key: different feeds can reuse an `event_id`. Keep each feed's checkpoint with that feed too.

A request after cursor `C` returns events with cursors greater than `C`, in order, up to the requested page limit. The response's `next_cursor` is the last event's cursor, or `C` if the response is empty. Although cursors increase monotonically, clients treat them as opaque tokens: store and resend them without doing arithmetic. The short cursor names below are illustrative.

Receiving `next_cursor` only tells you where the next request can start. It does not acknowledge any writes to your local database. There is no transaction spanning the feed service and that database.

## Apply events and save progress

Start with the local copy and the checkpoint that belongs to it. For a new copy, install a [fresh snapshot](snapshot.md) and its matching feed cursor together as one local checkpoint.

One supported arrangement commits each event's local change and processed ID together, then saves the page checkpoint separately. Use this loop:

1. Load the saved cursor for the feed and request a page after it.
2. Process the returned events in order. For each event, begin a local transaction and check its deduplication key in the processed-event record. If the key is present, skip its local effects. Otherwise, apply the local change and record the key in that same transaction. Commit the transaction before continuing.
3. Save the response's `next_cursor` only after every event in the page has either committed its change and processed ID or been recognized as already processed. If processing fails partway through, leave the checkpoint unchanged.
4. Request the next page after the saved cursor. After a restart, begin again at step 1 using the durable checkpoint.

The deduplication check, the change for an unseen event and its processed ID must be part of one local transaction. This makes a recorded ID evidence that its corresponding local change committed. Recording an ID first and applying the change later could cause a restart to skip a change that never happened. Applying the change without atomically recording its ID could cause a restart to apply it again.

The contract also supports committing the entire page's local changes, processed IDs and checkpoint in one local transaction. Perform the deduplication checks inside that transaction as well. This commits all the page's progress together; an uncommitted page leaves the previous checkpoint and local state in place.

### Why events can appear again

With a separately saved checkpoint, a crash can occur after an event's local transaction commits but before the checkpoint advances. The next request starts from the older checkpoint, so the feed returns that event again. Its processed ID lets the consumer skip its effects and continue through the page.

Saving the checkpoint before committing the corresponding work creates the opposite problem: after a crash, the request starts past events whose changes are still missing locally. Keep the checkpoint behind uncommitted work. While history remains available, a stale checkpoint can be recovered by replay and deduplication; a checkpoint saved ahead of the work can skip it.

## Worked example: matching payloads, distinct events

Consider the single-feed trace in the [consumer design notes](../notes/consumer-design.md). Call the feed `F`. The saved cursor is `c40`, and neither of the following events is recorded as processed. A request after `c40` returns this page with `next_cursor` equal to `c42`:

| `event_id` | Cursor | Item | Value | Timestamp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e41` | `c41` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |
| `e42` | `c42` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |

Assume the consumer uses per-event transactions and saves the checkpoint separately. To make the effects visible, it also maintains a local event count in the same transaction as each event's change and processed ID. The counts below show only the contribution from these two events.

1. The consumer applies `e41`, increments the count to 1 and records `(F, e41)`. Its local transaction commits.
2. The process exits before applying `e42` and before saving `c42`. The durable checkpoint is still `c40`; the local change for `e41` and its processed ID remain committed.
3. The consumer restarts and requests events after `c40`. While the events remain available, this returns `e41` and `e42` again.
4. For `e41`, the transactional check finds `(F, e41)`. This is repeated delivery of an already processed event, so the consumer skips its effects. The count stays at 1.
5. For `e42`, the transactional check finds no `(F, e42)`. This is a distinct accepted event despite its matching payload. The consumer applies it, increments the count to 2 and records `(F, e42)` in one committed transaction.
6. Both events are now processed, so the consumer saves checkpoint `c42`. The next request starts after `c42`.

If another crash happens after step 5 but before step 6, both events can arrive again. Both IDs are already recorded, so neither changes the count; the consumer can finish the page and save `c42`.

Deduplicating by item, value and timestamp would incorrectly discard `e42`. Applying every delivery without checking event identity would count `e41` again after the first restart. Using `(feed_id, event_id)` preserves both distinct events and suppresses their repeated deliveries.

## When the saved cursor has expired

Events remain available for 72 hours after server acceptance. If the requested cursor is before the available history, the server returns `history_expired`; replay from that checkpoint can no longer fill the gap.

Obtain a [fresh snapshot](snapshot.md) containing the current materialized state and its matching feed cursor. Replace the local copy with that state and install the matching cursor together as one local checkpoint. Then request events after that cursor.

This rebuilds the current local state. It cannot reconstruct expired event history, so it cannot recover a count of missed events from their individual deliveries, even if the materialized values look unchanged.

# Foldnote

Foldnote combines a folder of workshop notes into a single Markdown handout for sharing or printing from your Markdown editor.

## Quick start

You need **Python 3.11 or later**. Foldnote uses only the Python standard library and runs directly from the release folder.

Open a terminal in the release folder containing `foldnote.py` and `examples/`, then run:

```sh
python foldnote.py build examples/notes handout.md
```

This creates `handout.md` in the current folder from the bundled example notes. Open it in your Markdown editor to view, share, or print your first handout. Foldnote produces Markdown; it does not generate PDFs.

If `handout.md` already exists, the command stops without replacing it. Choose a new output filename, or use `--replace` when you intend to overwrite that file.

## Use your own notes

Replace `examples/notes` with the folder containing your Markdown notes. Keep the output path outside that folder. For example, if your notes are in a `notes` folder beside `foldnote.py`, run:

```sh
python foldnote.py build notes workshop-handout.md
```

Foldnote reads `.md` files recursively, orders them by their paths relative to the notes folder, and adds a heading showing each input path. Numbered filenames such as `01-welcome.md` and `02-tools.md` help set the order within a folder. The input notes remain unchanged.

Image references stay as written, and Foldnote does not copy image files. Check the image paths before sharing the handout.

## Documentation

- [Using Foldnote](docs/using-foldnote.md): command behavior and output options.
- [Contributing](docs/contributing.md): guidance for developers changing the tool.

Have the agent read the relevant `SKILL.md` and its applicable references. # Labelcards release update

## Decision

The disagreement came from the sort keys: `list_presets()` in [the CLI](labelcards.py) used `id`, while [the build](scripts/build_metadata.py) used `display_order`. A baseline build left the supplied generated files unchanged, ruling out stale output as the cause of this mismatch.

Both displays now follow `display_order`, as required by [the release brief](notes/release.md). The new `vial` record is 40 mm wide by 20 mm high with order 25, between `folder` and `shelf`. The existing records retain their dimensions and order values.

[Maintenance notes](docs/maintenance.md) identify `catalog.json` as the source for the CLI and generated files. # Restart-safe synchronization

To build a local copy from the Kite Ledger event feed, keep a durable checkpoint and a record of processed event IDs alongside your local data. After a restart, request events after the saved checkpoint. Some events may arrive again because their local changes committed before the checkpoint was saved. Use their IDs to recognize that replay and avoid applying the same event twice.

## Track position and event identity

The [feed contract](feed-contract.md) gives the cursor and the event ID different jobs:

- A **cursor** identifies a position in the ordered feed. A request after cursor `C` returns events with cursors greater than `C`, in order, up to the requested page limit. Your **checkpoint** is the cursor you durably save to resume from; it must not advance past uncommitted local work.
- An **event_id** identifies one accepted event. It is immutable and unique within its feed. A repeated delivery keeps the same ID. For a consumer of several feeds, use `(feed_id, event_id)` as the deduplication key because different feeds can reuse an ID.

The response's `next_cursor` is the cursor of its last event. It tells you where to request the next page; it does not acknowledge writes to your database. An empty response returns the requested cursor as `next_cursor`.

Treat cursors as opaque tokens: store and resend them without doing arithmetic. The short cursor names in the example below are illustrative.

Compare IDs to decide whether an event has already been processed. Payload fields cannot establish identity: two distinct accepted events can have the same item, value and timestamp. Deduplicating by those fields would discard valid events. A repeated delivery of one event should have one local effect; two distinct events must each be processed, even when their payloads match.

## Commit local changes and progress safely

For an initial copy, obtain a [fresh snapshot](snapshot.md) and install its materialized state and matching feed cursor as one local checkpoint. For an existing copy, load the saved checkpoint and processed IDs from durable storage.

The following loop uses the supported arrangement in which each event's local change and processed ID commit together, and the page checkpoint is saved separately. It follows the ordering described in the [consumer notes](../notes/consumer-design.md).

1. Request a page after the saved checkpoint.
2. Process each event in feed order. In a local transaction, check whether its deduplication key is already recorded. If it is, skip its local change. Otherwise, apply the change and record the key in that same transaction. Commit before moving to the next event.
3. After every event in the page has either committed or been recognized as already processed, durably save the response's `next_cursor` as the checkpoint.
4. Request the next page after that saved cursor. After a restart, begin again with the checkpoint actually saved to durable storage.

Keep the deduplication check, the local change and the processed-ID write inside the same transaction. Committing a processed ID separately before its local change can cause the restarted consumer to skip work that never took effect. Committing the change without its ID can cause the restarted consumer to apply that change again.

Keep the checkpoint behind any unfinished work. If you durably save a page's `next_cursor` while any of its local changes remain uncommitted, a crash can leave unapplied events behind the saved position. A request after that checkpoint will skip them. If an event fails to commit, do not advance the checkpoint past it.

A crash after an event transaction commits but before the checkpoint is saved leaves the checkpoint behind the local data. The next request can therefore return that event again. Its durable processed ID lets the consumer recognize the replay and skip the already committed change.

You can instead commit a whole page's local changes, processed IDs and `next_cursor` together in one local transaction. With that arrangement, a crash before the transaction commits leaves both the page's changes and checkpoint uncommitted; a successful commit saves them together. In either arrangement, keep the deduplication check with the local changes and ID records. These transactions cover local state; the feed service and local database do not share a transaction. See the [supported transaction arrangements](feed-contract.md).

## Worked example: identical payloads, distinct events

Consider the single-feed trace in the [consumer notes](../notes/consumer-design.md). The saved cursor is `c40`. A request after `c40` returns the following page, with `next_cursor` equal to `c42`:

| Event ID | Cursor | Item | Value | Timestamp |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `e41` | `c41` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |
| `e42` | `c42` | `shelf-A` | `6` | `10:05` |

Suppose the local transaction also maintains an event count, initially zero for these two events. The consumer saves the checkpoint separately from each event transaction:

1. The transaction for `e41` applies its local change, increments the count to one and records `e41` as processed. It commits.
2. The process exits before applying `e42` and before saving `c42`. The durable state still has checkpoint `c40`, processed ID `e41` and count one.
3. On restart, the consumer requests events after `c40`. The feed returns `e41` and `e42` again.
4. The transaction for the redelivered `e41` finds its processed ID and skips its change and count increment. The count stays at one.
5. The transaction for `e42` finds no processed ID, applies its change, increments the count to two and records `e42`. It commits.
6. Both events are now processed, so the consumer saves `c42` as its checkpoint. The next request is after `c42`.

The second delivery of `e41` repeats an event already applied locally. `e42` is a separate accepted event, so its matching payload must not cause it to be skipped. The final count is two: each distinct event counted once. If another crash happens after step 5 but before step 6, both IDs are already durable, so replaying the page leaves the count at two and allows the checkpoint to catch up.

## Recover when the saved cursor has expired

Events remain available for **72 hours after server acceptance**. If your saved cursor is before the available history, the server returns `history_expired`. Repeating the request with that cursor cannot recover the missing history.

Obtain a fresh snapshot with its matching feed cursor. Replace your local copy with the snapshot's materialized state and install that state and cursor as one local checkpoint. Then continue requesting events after that cursor, using the same transaction and deduplication rules. See the [snapshot contract](snapshot.md).

A snapshot rebuilds current materialized state. It cannot reconstruct expired event history, so it cannot recover a count or other result that requires those missing events.

# Пробное раннее открытие читальной комнаты «Тихий двор»

На 8 октября 2026 года

Раннее открытие получило положительный отклик в большинстве заполненных бланков. Однако пока неизвестно, сколько людей воспользовались дополнительным часом, поэтому оснований для постоянного изменения расписания недостаточно. Предлагаю продолжить пробу 10 и 17 октября и уточнить учёт посещений: на эти две субботы дежурных хватает.

## Что показали две субботы

Обычно комната работает по субботам с 10:30 до 13:00. 26 сентября и 3 октября её открывали в 9:30, сохранив время закрытия. По [сводке](../materials/pilot-summary.md), в эти дни зарегистрировали 14 и 12 посещений — всего 26. За две предшествующие субботы было 12 и 16 посещений, всего 28. В пробные дни общее число посещений не выросло, но такого короткого сравнения недостаточно, чтобы установить влияние раннего открытия на посещаемость.

Из 18 заполненных бланков в 13 раннее открытие названо удобным, в трёх время открытия не имело значения, в двух предложено попробовать вечерние часы. Это ответы, полученные за отдельные посещения: бланк выдавали при каждом посещении, и один человек мог ответить в обе субботы. Уникальных посетителей не считали, поэтому 13 положительных ответов нельзя приравнять к 13 разным людям.

В бланках спрашивали об удобстве расписания, но не отмечали время прихода. Ответы описывают отношение к расписанию, однако не показывают, сколько людей действительно пользовались комнатой до 10:30.

По [записям дежурных](../materials/session-records.md), перед открытием в обе пробные субботы очередь была короче обычной. Длину очереди и время ожидания не измеряли, поэтому это пока наблюдение, требующее проверки. В первую субботу шёл дождь; его обсуждали как возможное объяснение посещаемости, но влияние погоды отдельно не проверяли.

## Достаточно ли этого для решения о расписании

Отклик в бланках и наблюдения дежурных дают повод продолжить пробу. Для постоянного расписания нужно понять, используется ли дополнительный час в разные субботы и удастся ли обеспечить его дежурными. Сейчас нет учёта прихода до 10:30, неизвестно число разных посетителей, а наблюдение охватывает всего два дня. Предложение о вечерних часах также стоит сохранить для дальнейшего обсуждения, но два бланка сами по себе не обосновывают смену направления пробы.

## Предлагаемый следующий шаг

Предлагаю согласовать ещё две пробные субботы — 10 и 17 октября — с работой с 9:30 до 13:00. До следующей смены стоит договориться об учёте:

- отмечать время прихода и отдельно подсчитывать посещения, начавшиеся до 10:30;
- добавить в бланк вопрос, пользовался ли человек комнатой до 10:30;
- выбрать способ учёта повторных визитов без записи имён. В обсуждении уже предложен вопрос о посещении предыдущей пробной субботы; способ учёта ещё нужно согласовать.

Учёт времени прихода и новый вопрос в бланке предложил координатор смен, но эти изменения пока не утверждены. После 17 октября предлагаю сопоставить использование дополнительного часа по дням с ответами в бланках и обсудить, достаточно ли оснований для постоянного раннего открытия или нужны дополнительные наблюдения. Для работы после этих двух дат состав смен придётся согласовать заново. Постоянное расписание пока остаётся прежним.

# Maintenance window on JVI instrument hosts

For a complete restore procedure, including snapshot validation and recovery,
see [Restore a local EmberTS snapshot](restore-local-snapshot.md).

These hosts have two relevant systemd services:

- `jvi-ingest.service` is the only application writer to EmberTS on the host.
- `emberts.service` is the local database engine.

A managed stop of `jvi-ingest.service` finishes its current transaction, stops new submissions, and leaves it stopped until an operator starts it. Stopping the database alone does not place the application in maintenance. The ingestion service must remain stopped during an active-root change and its checks.

Before a restore window, the incident lead and data owner choose the snapshot and decide whether missing later commits are acceptable or require a separate replay plan. Snapshot restoration performs no replay. If the chosen snapshot does not satisfy the incident's data requirement, resolve that before activation.

Restoring into a separate root can be done while both services are running. For the actual change:

```sh
sudo systemctl stop jvi-ingest.service
sudo systemctl stop emberts.service
```

Capture the current root path and generation before activation. After activation, start only the database first:

```sh
sudo systemctl start emberts.service
sudo emberctl probe --format json
```

Keep ingestion stopped until the probe confirms readiness, the intended active root, and the selected snapshot ID and commit sequence. If the probe is not ready or names a different root, remain in maintenance and investigate. When the restored state is accepted, resume the writer:

```sh
sudo systemctl start jvi-ingest.service
```

## Returning to the former root

If activation has succeeded but the new root cannot be accepted, and ingestion has remained stopped throughout, stop the database again, inspect the current active metadata, and activate the saved former root using the current generation. Do not reuse the generation from before the first successful activation: every successful activation increments it. Confirm that the active metadata still describes the change you are handling before reversing it. Start the database, probe for readiness and the saved root path, then decide whether to resume ingestion.

Once ingestion has resumed, the restored root can contain new commits that are absent from the former root. Returning to the former root would omit those commits. If trouble appears at that point, stop ingestion and obtain a reconciliation or replay plan from the incident lead; the immediate pre-resume rollback procedure no longer establishes an acceptable data state.

See the [command reference](../reference/emberctl.md) and [snapshot design notes](../../notes/snapshot-design.md).

# Restore a local EmberTS snapshot

Use this runbook to restore a local snapshot on one Juniper Vale Instruments
host running EmberTS 4.2. The restore creates a separate database root; you then
pause ingestion and the database to make that root active. Staging can happen
while both services are running.

The restored database contains the committed view through the selected
snapshot's `commit_seq`. Restoration performs no replay of later commits.
Before activation, the incident lead and data owner must agree that this view
meets the incident's data requirement or establish a separate replay plan.

**Keep `jvi-ingest.service` stopped throughout activation and acceptance checks.**
You can return to the retained former root during that pause. Once ingestion
has resumed, the restored root can contain new commits absent from the former
root; returning to the former root then requires a reconciliation or replay
decision.

## Before you start

- Work on the host being restored. There is no remote restore mode. Have access
  to the selected snapshot directory and `sudo` access for systemd operations
  and commands that access `/var/lib/emberts`.
- Use a snapshot in format **7 or 8**. A snapshot is a directory containing a
  manifest and segment files, not a single archive.
- Choose a target that **does not exist** and is a direct child of
  `/var/lib/emberts/roots`. Supported roots and the active metadata at
  `/var/lib/emberts/ACTIVE` must be on the same local filesystem. Do not create
  the target directory in advance. Overwriting an existing root is unsupported.
- Keep the former live root available for recovery. Staging needs room for the
  new root and temporary workspace in addition to the space already occupied
  by the live root; activation does not free that space.

The [maintenance-window page](maintenance-window.md) explains the two services
and writer controls. Exact command behavior and exit codes are in the
[EmberTS 4.2 command reference](../reference/emberctl.md).

## Restore procedure

All commands below run on the target host. The paths, IDs, sizes, and generation
numbers shown are illustrative values from the
[worked example](../../examples/local-restore-session.txt). Substitute your
chosen paths and actual command results. Record the snapshot metadata, root
paths, generations, and verification results in the incident notes as you go.

### 1. Inspect and accept the snapshot's recovery point

Set the selected source and an unused target path:

```sh
SNAPSHOT=/srv/ember-snapshots/jvi-2026-09-21T0200.etsnap
TARGET=/var/lib/emberts/roots/recovery-2026-09-21
sudo emberctl snapshot inspect "$SNAPSHOT" --format json
```

The worked example has these manifest values:

```json
{
  "snapshot_id": "jvi-2026-09-21-a",
  "format_version": 8,
  "created_at": "2026-09-21T02:08:31Z",
  "commit_seq": 872110,
  "last_commit_at": "2026-09-21T01:59:54Z",
  "unpacked_bytes": 9663676416
}
```

Record `snapshot_id` and `commit_seq` for the post-start checks. Confirm that
`format_version` is 7 or 8; otherwise stop and use a compatible release under a
separate upgrade or migration procedure.

Use `commit_seq` to identify the last included transaction and `last_commit_at`
for its commit time. The example restores through sequence 872110, committed
at 01:59:54. Its `created_at` value of 02:08:31 records when packaging finished,
not a later recovery point. Event timestamps also do not determine inclusion:
a reading timestamped 01:55 but committed after
sequence 872110 is absent from this snapshot. See the
[snapshot design notes](../../notes/snapshot-design.md#what-is-captured) for
this distinction. Resolve the data requirement with the incident lead and data
owner before proceeding to activation.

Inspection reads the manifest only. It does not read every segment or validate
segment digests; the next step performs that validation.

### 2. Validate the snapshot, target, and free space

```sh
sudo emberctl restore "$SNAPSHOT" --target "$TARGET" --dry-run
```

Continue only when the command succeeds with `result=dry_run_ok`. The dry run
validates the manifest, supported format, all segment SHA-256 digests, target
location, and available space. It creates no target and changes no database
state.

The required free bytes are:

```text
unpacked_bytes + max(1073741824, ceil(0.05 * unpacked_bytes))
```

The additional term is the larger of 1 GiB and 5% of the unpacked size, rounded
up to whole bytes. For the example's 9 GiB snapshot, the requirement is 10 GiB:

```text
required_free_bytes=10737418240
available_free_bytes=21474836480
result=dry_run_ok
```

The live root's existing consumption is already reflected in the free-space
measurement. A successful dry run does not reserve space; the actual restore
checks the current source and free space again.

### 3. Stage the new root

```sh
sudo emberctl restore "$SNAPSHOT" --target "$TARGET"
```

Continue only on a successful `result=staged`. Restore writes the READY marker
only after the staged root is complete. This command neither changes the active
root nor stops either service.

If copying fails, an incomplete target can remain without a READY marker.
Do not activate it or retry into that existing path. Use a fresh, nonexistent
target for another attempt; review the incomplete directory separately before
deciding how to remove it. See [failures before a successful activation](#failures-before-a-successful-activation).

### 4. Pause the writer, then the database

```sh
sudo systemctl stop jvi-ingest.service
sudo systemctl stop emberts.service
```

The managed ingestion stop finishes its current transaction and stops new
submissions. Stopping only the database does not place the application in
maintenance. Confirm both services are stopped before continuing; if either
stop fails, resolve it before activation. Keep ingestion stopped through the
remaining checks and any return to the former root.

### 5. Save the former root and activate the staged root

Read the current metadata while the database is stopped:

```sh
sudo emberctl active --format json
```

Save **both** `active_root` and `generation`. Set the following variables from
that output; these values are the worked example, not defaults:

```sh
FORMER_ROOT=/var/lib/emberts/roots/live-44
BEFORE_GENERATION=44
```

Activate the staged root using the generation you just inspected:

```sh
sudo emberctl activate --target "$TARGET" --expect-generation "$BEFORE_GENERATION"
```

Activation requires a stopped database and an intact target with a READY
marker. On success it switches the active metadata and increments `generation`
by one. It retains the former root without modifying it and starts neither
service.

If activation fails, follow the [failure guidance](#failures-before-a-successful-activation)
before continuing. A generation mismatch means the state changed after your
inspection: inspect and resolve that change, rather than merely substituting
a newer number and retrying.

After successful activation, inspect and record the resulting metadata:

```sh
sudo emberctl active --format json
```

Expect `active_root` to equal `$TARGET` and `generation` to be one greater than
the saved value: 45 in the example. If the metadata differs, remain in
maintenance and resolve the unexpected change with the incident lead before
starting the database or reversing the change.

### 6. Start only the database and verify the restored state

```sh
sudo systemctl start emberts.service
sudo emberctl probe --format json
```

Keep ingestion stopped. Require all four probe checks:

| Probe field | Required result |
| --- | --- |
| `state` | `ready` |
| `active_root` | The intended `$TARGET` path |
| `restored_snapshot_id` | The `snapshot_id` recorded in step 1 (`jvi-2026-09-21-a` in the example) |
| `opened_commit_seq` | The `commit_seq` recorded in step 1 (`872110` in the example) |

`opened_commit_seq` is the position at which this service start opened the
root, not a count of writes arriving later. A successful systemd start alone
does not establish that the intended snapshot is open.

If the database fails to start, the probe is not ready, or any identity or
sequence check fails, leave ingestion stopped. **A successful activation has
already changed the active root even if the subsequent database start fails.**
Use [return to the former root](#return-to-the-former-root-before-ingestion-resumes)
if the restored root cannot be accepted.

### 7. Accept the restored state and resume ingestion

Once the probe checks pass and the restored state is accepted under the agreed
data requirement, resume the writer:

```sh
sudo systemctl start jvi-ingest.service
```

Confirm that ingestion is running and record that it has resumed. The restore
is complete when the database has passed the checks above and the writer is
running. Retain the former root; removing it is outside this restore procedure.
If ingestion fails to start, keep it stopped while investigating. If it may
have run at all, use the [post-resume recovery guidance](#trouble-after-ingestion-resumes).

## Failures before a successful activation

A staging failure does not change the active metadata. Every failed activation
also leaves the active metadata unchanged by that attempt. If the outcome is
unclear, inspect it with `sudo emberctl active --format json` instead of assuming
which root is active.

| Exit | Meaning and next action |
| --- | --- |
| `11` | Unsupported snapshot format. Stop; use a compatible release under a separate upgrade or migration procedure. No copying or activation occurred. |
| `12` | Invalid manifest or segment digest. No copying or activation occurred. Obtain an intact snapshot and confirm its recovery point with the incident lead and data owner before retrying. |
| `21` | Existing or unsupported target, or an activation target without the required readiness. Active metadata is unchanged. For staging, select a fresh, valid target; for activation, use an intact root with a READY marker. There is no overwrite or force option. |
| `22` | Insufficient free space. No copying or activation occurred. Resolve capacity and repeat the dry run; activation will not free the former root. |
| `25` | Staging copy failed. Active metadata is unchanged, but an incomplete directory may remain. Retry with a fresh target; review the incomplete directory separately before removal. |
| `31` | Database still running during activation. Active metadata is unchanged. Keep ingestion stopped, resolve the database stop, and inspect active metadata before deciding to retry. |
| `32` | Generation mismatch. Active metadata is unchanged by this attempt. Inspect the current root and generation and resolve the concurrent change with the incident lead or other operator. A newer generation is not permission to repeat the original decision. |

If you abandon the change after stopping services but before a successful
activation, inspect the active metadata and confirm it still identifies the
saved former root and expected generation. If it does, start the database and
probe for `state=ready` and the former root path before deciding to resume
ingestion. If it does not, resolve the unexpected state before proceeding.

## Return to the former root before ingestion resumes

Use this procedure only if activation succeeded, the new root cannot be
accepted, and **ingestion has remained stopped throughout**. The saved former
root must remain intact with its READY marker.

1. Leave ingestion stopped and stop the database again:

   ```sh
   sudo systemctl stop emberts.service
   ```

2. Inspect the current active metadata:

   ```sh
   sudo emberctl active --format json
   ```

   Confirm that the root and generation still describe the activation you are
   reversing. If either differs from the recorded post-activation state, stop
   and resolve the concurrent change before reversing anything. Set the rollback
   generation from this fresh inspection. In the worked example:

   ```sh
   ROLLBACK_GENERATION=45
   ```

   Do not reuse `BEFORE_GENERATION`: each successful activation increments the
   generation, including a return to a former root.

3. Activate the saved former root:

   ```sh
   sudo emberctl activate --target "$FORMER_ROOT" --expect-generation "$ROLLBACK_GENERATION"
   ```

   On success, inspect the metadata again:

   ```sh
   sudo emberctl active --format json
   ```

   Confirm the former root path and the incremented generation: 46 in the
   example. If activation fails or the metadata is unexpected, leave ingestion
   stopped and escalate rather than continuing to restart services.

4. Start the database and verify the former root:

   ```sh
   sudo systemctl start emberts.service
   sudo emberctl probe --format json
   ```

   Require `state=ready` and `active_root` equal to the saved `$FORMER_ROOT`.
   An ordinary former live root may have a null `restored_snapshot_id`; do not
   apply the selected snapshot's ID and sequence checks to this rollback.

5. If the former root is ready, decide with the incident lead whether to resume
   ingestion, then run:

   ```sh
   sudo systemctl start jvi-ingest.service
   ```

   Confirm ingestion is running. If the former database cannot start or its
   probe fails, keep ingestion stopped and escalate.

## Trouble after ingestion resumes

Stop ingestion:

```sh
sudo systemctl stop jvi-ingest.service
```

Obtain a reconciliation or replay plan from the incident lead, with the data
owner involved in the data decision. Do not apply the immediate rollback above
as though the two roots were equivalent. New commits in the restored root can
be absent from the former root, and no background process makes the roots
converge. Stopping ingestion now does not undo that divergence.

For escalation, provide the selected snapshot ID and commit sequence, staged
target, saved former root, recorded and current generations, failing command
and exit status, available probe output, and whether ingestion has resumed or
its state is uncertain. Remain in maintenance when readiness, root identity,
or the acceptable data state is unresolved.

# Replace audio

Use a corrected mix in your existing ListenDraft review while keeping its title, review link, and sharing settings. You must be the review owner or an Editor. You can also replace audio in an `Approved` review.

## Choose what happens to comments

`Carry comments forward` is on by default. Leave it on to keep general comments and timed threads whose timestamps are before the new audio’s end. Carried threads keep their timestamps, replies, and open or resolved state.

This works well for a corrected mix with unchanged timing. ListenDraft does not move comments to follow edits: if you shorten an introduction, a comment may point to the wrong moment. Consider turning the checkbox off if your edit shifts the timeline.

Timed threads at or beyond the new audio’s end stay with the previous revision in [Version history](version-history.md). With the checkbox off, all existing comments stay there and the new revision starts without them. Neither choice deletes comment history.

## Replace the file

1. On the current review page, open the `⋯` menu.
2. Choose `Replace audio`.
3. Select a file that meets the [Upload audio](upload-audio.md) requirements.
4. Set `Carry comments forward` using the guidance above.
5. Select `Replace`.
6. Wait until the page displays `Ready`.

Until processing succeeds, the previous audio remains current. Cancelled uploads, rejected files, and processing failures leave the previous audio, comments, and approval unchanged. See [Upload audio](upload-audio.md) for rejection and processing recovery steps.

## Request a new review

Every successful replacement has the status `Needs review`, regardless of the comment setting. Any previous approval stays in history; reviewers must approve the new audio.

Share the existing review link again when it is ready. ListenDraft does not notify reviewers automatically. Listeners with the page already open need to refresh to load the replacement; playback does not switch mid-listen. Only owners and Editors can browse Version history; reviewers see the current revision.
